title: Syncope and Transient Loss of Consciousness: Risk Stratification and Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults over 16 years with transient loss of consciousness (TLoC) in the emergency department (ED) or primary care: structured history and examination, 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), recognition of red flags for cardiac syncope, orthostatic hypotension, uncomplicated faint, features of epileptic seizure, ED disposition, specialist referral and driving advice. Uses the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 2018 syncope guideline and NICE CG109. Treatment of the specific arrhythmia or structural cause is in other topics.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi syncope guideline was found.
The ESC 2018 high-risk and low-risk feature table (Table 6) could not be read reliably from the opened copy; NICE CG109 red flags are used for urgent referral instead.
NICE CG109 gives no numeric threshold for orthostatic hypotension; the ESC 2018 definition is used.
Saudi Arabia driving rules after syncope were not found; NICE advice refers to UK rules and local traffic regulations apply.
Typical adult normal values for haemoglobin, troponin and D-dimer are not from these guidelines; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Syncope is TLoC from cerebral hypoperfusion; the main groups are reflex, orthostatic hypotension and cardiac syncope (ESC 2018, Table 5). Reflex (vasovagal) syncope follows posture, provoking factors and prodrome: the 3 Ps (NICE CG109, Section 1.1 uncomplicated faint). Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall in blood pressure on standing that reproduces symptoms (ESC 2018, p. 1902). Cardiac syncope comes from arrhythmia or structural heart disease and carries the highest short-term risk (ESC 2018, Table 5 and p. 1894).

symptoms: Prodrome of sweating or feeling warm before TLoC in reflex syncope (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Sudden palpitations before syncope suggest cardiac cause (ESC 2018, Table 5).
Syncope during exertion or when lying down suggests cardiac cause (ESC 2018, Table 5).
Prodromal déjà vu or jamais vu, or confusion afterwards, suggests epileptic seizure (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
physicalSigns: Heart murmur (NICE CG109, Section 1.1 red flags).
Signs of heart failure (NICE CG109, Section 1.1 red flags).
Fall in blood pressure on standing (ESC 2018, p. 1902).
Bitten tongue (side), head-turning, unusual posturing or prolonged limb jerking suggest seizure (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
redFlags: ECG abnormality: urgent cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Heart failure, TLoC during exertion, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur: urgent cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Age over 65 with TLoC and no prodrome: consider urgent cardiovascular assessment (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Family history of unexplained sudden death at a young age or known structural or coronary heart disease (ESC 2018, Table 5).
precipitants: Prolonged standing, pain or medical procedures in reflex syncope (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Straining during micturition, coughing or swallowing in situational syncope (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Medicines such as diuretics (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Haemorrhage, hypoxia, ischaemia or pulmonary embolism as acute causes (ESC 2018, p. 1894).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Posture, provoking factor and prodrome present, normal assessment (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Clearly and consistently provoked by micturition, cough or swallowing (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic, or systolic below 90 mmHg on standing with symptoms (ESC 2018, p. 1902).
Exertional or supine onset, palpitations, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease (ESC 2018, Table 5).
Lateral tongue bite, head-turning, posturing, prolonged jerking, post-event confusion, déjà vu (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Suspected from history; refer for neurological assessment (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Bundle branch block, any heart block, long or short QT, ST or T wave abnormality
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Any of these is a red flag for urgent cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
ruleIn.normalValue: Sinus rhythm 60 to 100 per minute, PR 120 to 200 ms, QRS below 120 ms, corrected QT interval (QTc) below about 450 ms (men) or 460 ms (women)

references.title: NICE CG109: Transient loss of consciousness ('blackouts') in over 16s (2010, amended 2023), Recommendations

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, diastolic 10 mmHg or more, or systolic below 90 mmHg
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms orthostatic syncope if it reproduces symptoms (ESC 2018, p. 1902; NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
ruleIn.normalValue: Systolic fall below 20 mmHg and diastolic fall below 10 mmHg on standing

clinicalManagement.title: Take a structured history
actions: Record circumstances, posture just before, prodrome, tongue biting (side or tip), duration and witness account (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
Record current medicines that may have contributed, such as diuretics (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Examine and record an ECG
actions: Examine heart rate, lying and standing blood pressure and heart sounds; record a 12-lead ECG (NICE CG109, Section 1.1; ESC 2018, p. 1902).
Request blood tests only for a specific suspicion: haemorrhage, hypoxia, ischaemia or embolism (ESC 2018, p. 1894).

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify risk
actions: Any NICE red flag: urgent cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
ECG criteria for arrhythmic syncope: treat as cardiac syncope (ESC 2018, p. 1894).
High-risk patients: early intensive evaluation in a syncope unit or ED observation unit, or admission (ESC 2018, p. 1896; class I).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge low-risk patients
actions: Low-risk patients with likely reflex, situational or orthostatic syncope can be discharged (ESC 2018, p. 1896; class I).
Neither high nor low risk: observe in the ED or syncope unit rather than admit (ESC 2018, p. 1896).
Uncomplicated faint with normal assessment needs no further immediate management (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer suspected seizures
actions: One or more seizure features: refer to an epilepsy specialist, seen within 2 weeks (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Advise on driving
actions: Give driving advice at first presentation; the person must not drive while awaiting specialist assessment (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine is indicated for the ED assessment of syncope. Treat any specific cause (arrhythmia, bleeding, embolism) in its own pathway. Review and stop contributing medicines such as diuretics (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Arrhythmic syncope highly probable on ECG
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Persistent sinus bradycardia below 40 per minute or pauses over 3 seconds while awake, Mobitz II or higher atrioventricular block, alternating bundle branch block, ventricular or rapid supraventricular tachycardia, non-sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, long or short QT, or pacemaker malfunction with pauses (ESC 2018, p. 1894; class I).
Progressive, sustained fall in systolic blood pressure of 20 mmHg or more, diastolic 10 mmHg or more, or systolic below 90 mmHg on standing, reproducing symptoms (ESC 2018, p. 1902; class I).
Posture, provoking factor and prodrome with no features of another diagnosis (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).

teaching.scope: Adults over 16 years with transient loss of consciousness (TLoC) in the emergency department (ED) or primary care: structured history and examination, 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), recognition of red flags for cardiac syncope, orthostatic hypotension, uncomplicated faint, features of epileptic seizure, ED disposition, specialist referral and driving advice. Uses the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 2018 syncope guideline and NICE CG109. Treatment of the specific arrhythmia or structural cause is in other topics.
learningObjectives: Use the 12-lead ECG and red flags to find cardiac syncope.
Diagnose orthostatic hypotension with standing blood pressure.
Know who can go home and who needs referral within 24 hours.
pitfalls: Discharging a patient with an abnormal ECG.
Ordering CT head for every faint.
Labelling a faint as epilepsy because of brief jerks.
keyPoints: The 3 Ps point to an uncomplicated faint.
Exertional or supine syncope is cardiac until proven otherwise.
Brief jerking can occur in a faint; prolonged jerking suggests seizure.
Routine CT head has low yield.

patientEducation: Most faints are harmless; lie down with legs raised at the first warning signs.
Do not drive until a doctor says it is safe.
Return at once for blackout on exertion, chest pain or palpitations.
lifestyleAndDiet: Drink enough fluid and avoid prolonged standing in heat if you have reflex syncope.
Stand up slowly if you have orthostatic hypotension.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; cardiologist or syncope unit; epilepsy specialist for seizure features; general practitioner (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
dischargeCriteria: Low-risk features only, normal ECG, likely reflex, situational or orthostatic cause, driving advice given, general practitioner informed (ESC 2018, p. 1896; NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Red flags: cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours; seizure features: epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks; uncomplicated faint: general practitioner with the ECG record (NICE CG109, Section 1.1).
